title: The hypertrophy series: surpassing cardiovascular limitations
summary: NH explains that poor cardiovascular conditioning makes you end sets before your muscles fail, costing tonnage and size. Instead of separate cardio, he builds lifting-specific conditioning with supersets and giant sets (about 80% of his training), which lets him train 2-3 hours a day, 6 days a week, without gassing out.

claims.claim: The goal is to fail at the muscle, not at the cardiovascular system that feeds it; conditioning must never be the limiting factor.
Without stamina you can't build high lower-body tonnage, because heavy squats and deadlifts for many reps make you gas out.
On 20-rep squats ('widow makers') with a challenging weight, you're usually stopped by breathing, not your muscles.
Consistently failing to finish sets or workouts from poor conditioning means lost tonnage and, ultimately, lost size.
Former athletes in highly conditioned sports (wrestling, football, basketball) build work capacity easily when they start lifting.
Work capacity is essential for muscle growth because it lets you do the volume that drives it; it can be built and lost, and needs maintaining.
Before lifting he built work capacity with uphill sprints and morning runs, but sport-specific stamina isn't specific enough for lifting.
Lifters should build conditioning (GPP) within their program, using the movements of their own discipline.
For bodybuilders, supersets and giant sets are the answer: pair isolation movements that don't interfere with each other and do them non-stop.
About 80% of his training is done as giant sets, organised so muscles don't hinder each other while the heart and lungs are taxed throughout.
The heart and lungs serve the whole body, so giant sets of any muscle groups build cardiovascular endurance that carries over to strength work.
He deadlifts up to 5 reps and squats up to 8 reps at max weights without ever gassing out or needing 5 minutes between sets to recover his breath.
Because giant sets use working weights, conditioning rises alongside strength as the weights get heavier.
He hasn't done cardio in three years but has excellent stamina, which lets him train 2-3 hours a day, 6 days a week, and keep gaining.

Cardiovascular and muscular capacity should be balanced; being a cardio machine is pointless for muscle growth if you never push muscular endurance, and excess conditioning won't hinder growth the way unfinished sets do.
